codex.worst_flaw: The pilot’s safety audit samples only credited jobs, leaving unsafe starts among jobs with late or missing checklists outside its scope.

claude.worst_flaw: Team goals use a flat 70% target and don't handle small teams, uneven job volume or case mix, and there is no sample-size or uncertainty plan for the two-wave comparison over weeks 3 and 4.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with union buy-in, team-level paid-time reward, staggered rollout for evaluation, and data-integrity safeguards, but a 30-minute reward is modest and durability depends on whether workflow fixes alone sustain use once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot leaves crew assignment and the comparison window unclear, so differences in crew readiness or staggered workflow changes could be mistaken for a reward effect.

claude.worst_flaw: The 2-week staggered overlap with crew-level clustering on roughly 300 technicians is underpowered and pre-specifies no harms or cost outcomes, and the audit/appeal trail lacks replayable event history, versioned policy or independent shadow validation.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid setup, friction fixes, safety-hold credit and kill-switch guardrails make it approvable, but the modest meal reward and a lengthy multi-step measurement process may limit attention, while keeping the easier workflow after rewards end should help durability.

claude.worst_flaw: In a unionised workforce, a shared crew meal tied to a flat 65% threshold and crew progress posted at the weekly huddle can create peer pressure on individual technicians. The design does not test or mitigate that pressure, the 65% target is not tied to each crew's baseline, and the two-week staggered comparison has no stated sample size, uncertainty, or predefined harm outcomes.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the quality audit can independently detect omitted hazards, because the current audit can award credit for a false clearance when the technician leaves the hazard off the checklist.

holistic.reason: It's a careful, union-friendly design that rewards valid completion rather than clearance, fixes the workflow first, and has audit, dispute and staged-rollout safeguards, but a meal for a 65% crew threshold is a modest incentive, and lasting change depends on the workflow fixes holding after rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: There is effectively no comparison. Randomizing two ownership groups for two weeks gives only one unit per arm, and week 9-12 decisions rest on an 80% threshold with no uncertainty handling, no case-mix adjustment for PR size or complexity, and no limit on the group reward pressuring people into thin approvals beyond a five-PR weekly sample.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot can declare success on faster reviews without checking whether reviewers miss more defects or whether protected review time displaces other work.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck (reviewer time, coverage, queue) before adding a small, non-punitive reward with a randomized pilot and quality sampling, which suits sceptical engineers; however, the one-credit-per-review and one-hour reward is low-salience, the rules are fairly complex, and the weekly sampling and miscount handling add manager overhead.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward comparison uses only two rotations and leaves differences in pull request complexity, cross-rotation reviewing, and uncertainty unaddressed, so it cannot reliably isolate the reward’s effect.

claude.worst_flaw: The two-rotation reward comparison has only two clusters, is contaminated by cross-rotation reviewing, and defines no prior outcome threshold, cost or harm decision, so it cannot isolate how much the reward adds over plain workflow support.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, with a fair rule, private feedback, quality checks and a clear end plan, but the reward is a modest paid hour and the rule is complex enough that engineers may not notice it. The lasting gains depend on the routing and protected review time staying in place.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design falls back to an uncontrolled before-and-after comparison whenever the two groups share reviewers, which on a 25-engineer team is likely. In that case the reward's added value can't be separated from the workflow fixes, there is no sample size or uncertainty handling, and no costs or harms are set in advance as decision criteria.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward metric is not ready for launch because the design never specifies how submitted reviews are classified as useful before they receive credit.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottlenecks first, keeps rewards team-level, private and non-competitive, and has an explicit decision rule and quality guard, but it is long and complex to administer (counting rules, sampling, calendar edge cases) and the 60-minute learning-time reward is modest.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk launch decision lacks a valid measure of logging uptake or workflow value because audited hand-hygiene compliance can improve independently of kiosk use.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk logging the hospital wants adopted is never given a defined outcome or validated against the audits, so the design never shows whether the kiosk adds value. Audit corrections and appeals also have no replayable record or staffed appeal process.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, with a ward-level reward tied to existing audits, safeguards against gaming, a staggered rollout and no quotas. But a shared meal is a weak, diffuse motivator that few nurses will notice or respond to, and the kiosk habit likely fades once rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot decides whether to keep the kiosk using audited hand-hygiene compliance without measuring what fraction of eligible moments nurses log or whether those logs add enough value to justify the extra work.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk logging the hospital asked for has no defined target, credit or quality measure, so the programme rewards audited compliance and leaves the logging data largely unvalidated against observed behaviour.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, audit-based reward with pause rules, baseline-relative targets and staggered evaluation, but the small team meal, a kiosk that carries no incentive, and just three wards limit employee pull and durable change.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no replayable event log, versioned policy record or staffed appeal path; one ward champion handles every dispute, so ward-level meal awards cannot be independently corrected or audited.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot can award rewards even when sparse monthly audits miss a clinically important decline in hand-hygiene compliance.

holistic.reason: The design is thoughtful on safety guardrails, verification and fixing kiosk friction first, but it is complex (sampled-audit gating, staggered rewards, multi-threshold decisions), and ward-level meal rewards tied to observer-verified entries risk gaming and weak individual salience, though the lasting workflow simplification should keep some behaviour.

codex.worst_flaw: Customer-data exposure is a launch blocker because the design allows articles to count upon publication without a required privacy check, and the weekly QA sample can miss disclosures.

claude.worst_flaw: The randomised comparison covers only two weeks (weeks 3–4) across a handful of teams in a 60-person org, and no sample size, uncertainty handling or predefined cost/harm decision rule is set, so the incremental effect of the reward cannot be credibly separated from noise.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with a strong rollout, CSAT safeguards, QA sampling and a clear post-reward decision rule, but a 30-minute team break is a weak incentive and lasting change depends on the workflow fixes sticking after rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout rule is unready for launch because it counts tickets where linking would be inappropriate as misses and leaves unclear whether queue-specific milestones override the 35% threshold.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leaves the existing CSAT bonus untouched without checking whether it already discourages time spent on articles, uses only a single 10-ticket weekly sample and a manual correction channel instead of replayable event records with a staffed appeal, and compares two staggered team groups too small to separate the reward effect from queue mix.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with a fair all-ticket denominator, quality sampling, guardrails on handling time and CSAT, and a staggered comparison that tests lasting effect, but the reward is modest and the rules are complex enough that some agents may not notice or engage.

codex.worst_flaw: The 35% payout and continuation threshold has no feasibility baseline by case mix, so teams with fewer viable article opportunities can miss it even when agents use the knowledge base well.

claude.worst_flaw: Each team's reward depends on a 35% qualifying rate that has no cap on credit per article and is checked by a sample of only 10 tickets a week, so agents can attach the same generic article to many tickets and weak links can earn the reward. Meanwhile a CSAT drop is only reviewed, not paused, and its cause is not separated from case mix.

holistic.reason: It is a well-designed programme with a clear rule, workflow fixes, quality and CSAT guardrails and a randomised stagger, but the 35% team-level lunch reward is modest, the shared reward invites free-riding, and the habit depends on the workflow fixes sticking once the reward ends.
